title: Manthara
hook: a battlefield promise the king forgot, and a maid who remembered
carry: the rest will be done by a promise

segments.voice: Yesterday: Manthara painted a future where Bharata is lost, and Kaikeyi, after pushing back, asked how to stop it. Today, an old promise. A new week begins.

Years before Rama was born, the gods went to war with a demon named Shambara and asked King Dasharatha to fight beside them. Kaikeyi rode with him. The king was badly wounded and fell unconscious, and Kaikeyi drove his chariot out of the fighting and saved his life. When he woke, he said: ask me for two things, anything. I'll ask later, she said. And then, it seems, she forgot. Manthara didn't.
screen: `A WAR WITH SHAMBARA.` → `KAIKEYI SAVES THE KING.` → `ASK ME FOR TWO THINGS.`

segments.voice: Kaikeyi asks how to stop the coronation, and Manthara answers with Kaikeyi's own story. Don't you remember? You told it to me yourself. The king owes you two boons. Ask now. First, that Bharata be consecrated as heir. Second, that Rama be sent to the Dandaka forest for fourteen years, living as an ascetic: long enough, Manthara reasons, for Bharata to win the people's hearts and put down roots. Then the plan, step by step. Go to the anger room, where a wronged queen goes. Take off your jewels, put on soiled clothes, lie on the bare floor. When the king comes, don't look at him, don't speak. He can't bear to see you upset. He'll offer gems and gold; refuse them. Make him swear first, and only then ask. It's unsettling because it's so practical. Manthara knows the king's heart better than he does: his love for Kaikeyi, and his pride in keeping his word. She builds the trap out of those two good things. Kaikeyi, fully won, praises her warmly and promises her gold ornaments when Bharata rules. Then she does exactly as she's told: into the anger room, jewelry scattered on the floor, and down onto the bare floor. Manthara's part is done. The rest will be done by a promise.
screen: `THE KING OWES YOU TWO BOONS.` · `BHARATA CROWNED, RAMA TO THE FOREST.` · `GO TO THE ANGER ROOM.` · `A TRAP MADE OF GOOD THINGS.` · then, large: `THE REST WILL BE DONE BY A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Think of a promise someone made to you that you've never collected, or one you made that someone else still holds. Don't decide anything about it; just hold it lightly and notice its weight. On each breath out, let the shoulders drop.
Manthara. The maid who remembers the king's forgotten battlefield promise, and turns it, with a careful plan, into a trap.
Your line: the rest will be done by a promise. Tomorrow, the king walks in. Day five hundred nineteen, done.

howItsDone: The kopa-griha, or anger room, appears in this episode of the Ayodhya Kanda; storytellers often pause here to point out how Manthara builds her plan from the king's love and his pride in keeping his word.

original.note: Sanskrit krodhāgāra: the anger room, from krodha, anger, and āgāra, room or house.

trapdoor: what you thought: Kaikeyi invented the boons on the spot.
what it means: they were real, given after she saved the king in the war with Shambara, and Manthara reminded her.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki gives the fourteen-year term inside Manthara's plan, with a political reason: long enough for Bharata to take root.

chat.says: Wait, where did Kaikeyi's two wishes even come from?
options: The king promised them years ago, after she saved his life in battle.
Manthara made them up that night to trick the king into a deal.
The gods granted them to Kaikeyi on the morning of the coronation.
chat.meaning: Kaikeyi saved Dasharatha in the war with Shambara, and he offered her two boons. Manthara reminded her of them.

Shambara.meaning: the demon the gods fought, with Dasharatha's help

Dandaka.meaning: the great forest of Rama's exile

Manthara.meaning: Kaikeyi's maid from her old home

recall: the sage who answers Valmiki's question

notes: Sarga number follows the common (vulgate) numbering; confirm.
Details of the Shambara war (Kaikeyi drives the wounded, unconscious king from the field): confirm. Some versions have her repairing the chariot; that version is not used.
Manthara's reason for fourteen years (Bharata takes root): paraphrased; confirm.
Kaikeyi's praise of Manthara (including remarks about her hump) is softened to 'praises her warmly and promises gold ornaments'.
Valmiki's simile for Kaikeyi lying on the floor is left out because its wording could not be confirmed.
